title: Turn down the temperature
hook: Cool a chatbot from temperature 1 to 0.5. What happens to its top word’s chance?

knows: that a language model gives each possible next word a chance

misconception: Higher temperature makes a model more creative by adding new ideas; lower temperature makes it smarter.
objective: The learner can explain that temperature rescales the same scores, so cooler makes the top word more likely and hotter flattens the odds, and that it never adds a word the model had no score for.

claims.text: The toy has three candidate next words for “The cat sat on the …”: mat, sofa and moon, with invented scores 2, 1 and 0.
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (WORDS).

claims.text: Each word's chance is proportional to e^(score ÷ temperature), divided by the sum over the candidate words (softmax with temperature).
claims.source: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015, “Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network”, arXiv:1503.02531, eq. 1 (q_i = exp(z_i/T) / Σ_j exp(z_j/T)); implemented in probs() in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: For scores 2, 1, 0 the top word's chance is 86.7% at temperature 0.5, 66.5% at 1 and 41.9% at 4 (the three temperatures on the stage).
claims.source: e.g. T = 0.5: e⁴ : e² : e⁰ = 54.6 : 7.39 : 1, so 54.6 / 63.0 = 0.867. All five reproduced by running probs() from Demo.tsx. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node softmax of 2,1,0: T 0.5 -> 86.7%, T 1 -> 66.5%, T 4 -> 41.9% (the buttons Cool 0.5, Warm 1, Hot 4); reveal prints pct(probs(T)[0]).

claims.text: Dividing the scores 2, 1, 0 by 0.5 gives 4, 2, 0, doubling the gaps, and bigger gaps give more lopsided chances; dividing by 4 gives 0.5, 0.25, 0, and the chances drift toward a third each.
claims.source: Ratios of chances are e^((s_i − s_j)/T), so halving T squares each ratio; as T → ∞ every ratio → 1. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Reveal sentence matches; 2,1,0 / 0.5 = 4,2,0 and / 4 = 0.5,0.25,0; chances 41.9/32.6/25.4 at T 4 drift toward 1/3 (33.7/33.3/33.0 at T 100, own run).

claims.text: Temperature never adds or removes a word: at every temperature the same three words have a chance above zero.
claims.source: e^(s/T) > 0 for every finite score and T > 0, and the candidate list is fixed.

claims.text: Each temperature button (0.5, 1, 4) samples 20 words using that temperature's chances (seeded random numbers), and the reveal reports the learner's own counts at 0.5 and at 4.
claims.source: pick() and draw20() in Demo.tsx, seed 31; counts depend on press order but are deterministic for a given order. | draw20() in Demo.tsx, seed 31. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): pick() sets T and calls draw20 with probs(t) on the shared rng(31) stream; reveal prints drawsAt[0.5] and drawsAt[4] (gate requires both visits). Own re-run: order 0.5 then 4 gives 17/3/0 and 9/6/5; sampling frequencies over 100k draws match the chances (0.421/0.328/0.251 at T 4).

claims.text: About real systems: language models sample text with the same temperature setting, dividing the next-token scores by the temperature before the softmax.
claims.source: Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes & Choi 2020, “The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration”, ICLR 2020, arXiv:1904.09751 (describes sampling with temperature, dividing logits by t before the softmax, as a standard decoding method). Section number not checked: fact-checker to confirm.

claims.text: A hot model does not learn anything new; it only spreads its choices, picking unlikely words more often.
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 2. As a statement about the toy it is true (temperature only reweights fixed scores, c5). As a statement about real language models it is an interpretation: Peeperkorn et al. 2024 (ICCC), 'Is temperature the creativity parameter of large language models?', report, as I recall and have not re-read, only a weak correlation of temperature with novelty and a moderate one with incoherence, which supports 'not much more inventive' but not a flat 'not'. Needs a source or softer wording ('does not make the model learn anything new'). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. DISPUTED 2026-10-13: True of the toy, but stated as a flat fact about hot models. Peeperkorn et al. 2024 (ICCC; arXiv 2405.00492) report a weak positive link of temperature with novelty (beta about 0.31) and a moderate reduction in coherence, so 'not more inventive' is too strong. Fix: 'does not make the model learn anything new; it only spreads its choices'. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Was 'A hot model is not more inventive' (disputed: Peeperkorn et al. 2024 find a weak positive link of temperature with novelty). Narrowed to what temperature mechanically does. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Rechecked: narrowed to the mechanical effect on the toy (scores fixed, only probabilities reweighted); no longer a claim about novelty of real models.

claims.text: Each word's row shows its score divided by the current temperature (for example 2÷0.5=4); those divided scores are what the softmax uses.
claims.source: Stage label in Demo.tsx (score ÷ T), consistent with probs() and c2. | Added 2026-10-14 (v3) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Stage row label '{score}÷{T}={div(score)}' (2 dp), e.g. 2÷0.5=4, 1÷4=0.25; probs() exponentiates score / T.

recall.question: You raise a chatbot's temperature. What changes?
options: Less likely words get picked more often
It learns new words and ideas
recall.why: Temperature rescales the model's existing scores. Hotter flattens the odds toward unlikely choices; it adds nothing the model did not already score.
